title: Chapter 36
paragraphs: Daylight came. I rose at dawn. I spent an hour or two arranging my things in drawers and wardrobe—in the order I'd want to leave them during a short absence. Meanwhile, I heard St. John leave his room. He stopped at my door. I feared he would knock—no, but a slip of paper was pushed under the door. I picked it up. It read:

"You left me too suddenly last night. Had you stayed a little longer, you would have placed your hand on the Christian's cross and the angel's crown. I shall expect your clear decision when I return in two weeks. Meanwhile, watch and pray that you do not fall into temptation: the spirit, I trust, is willing, but the flesh, I see, is weak. I shall pray for you hourly.—Yours, ST. JOHN."

"My spirit," I answered silently, "is willing to do what is right. And my flesh, I hope, is strong enough to carry out Heaven's will, once that will is clearly known to me. At any rate, it shall be strong enough to search—to inquire—to find a way out of this cloud of doubt, and reach the open day of certainty."

It was the first of June, yet the morning was overcast and cold. Rain beat hard against my window. I heard the front door open and St. John walk out. Looking through the window, I saw him cross the garden. He took the path over the misty moors toward Whitcross—where he would catch the coach.
"In a few hours I'll follow you on that road, cousin," I thought. "I too have a coach to catch at Whitcross. I too have people to see and ask after in England before I leave forever."

It was still two hours until breakfast. I filled the time walking softly around my room, pondering the experience that had given my plans their new direction. I recalled the sensation I had felt—for I could recall it, with all its indescribable strangeness. I recalled the voice I had heard. Again I asked where it had come from, as uselessly as before. It had seemed to be inside me—not in the external world. I asked myself whether it was just a nervous impression—a hallucination. I couldn't believe so. It seemed more like an inspiration. The extraordinary effect on me confirmed this. I felt as though I had been called—not by mortal voice, but by something higher.
"Before many days," I said, ending my reflections, "I will know something of the man whose voice seemed to summon me last night. Letters have failed—I will go in person."
At breakfast I announced to Diana and Mary that I was going on a journey and would be away at least four days.
"Alone, Jane?" they asked.
"Yes. I need to see or hear news of a friend I've been worried about for some time."

They might have pointed out—as I'm sure they thought—that they'd believed I had no friends but them. I had often said as much. But with their genuine tact, they held back from commenting. Diana only asked if I was sure I was well enough to travel. I looked very pale, she observed. I replied that nothing was wrong except anxiety, which I hoped to relieve soon.

It was easy to make my arrangements. No one pestered me with questions or suspicions. Having explained that I couldn't yet share my plans, they kindly and wisely respected my silence. They granted me the freedom I would have given them under similar circumstances.

I left Moor House at three in the afternoon. Soon after four I stood at the Whitcross signpost, waiting for the coach that would take me to distant Thornfield. In the silence of those lonely roads and empty hills, I heard it approaching from far away. It was the same coach from which, a year ago, I had stepped down on this very spot—utterly lost, hopeless, and purposeless! It stopped at my signal. I climbed in—this time not forced to hand over my last coins for the fare. Once I had been penniless. Now I had means. The coach carried me away.

It was a journey of thirty-six hours. I had set out from Whitcross on a Tuesday afternoon. Early Thursday morning the coach stopped to water the horses at a roadside inn, set amid scenery whose green hedges, broad fields, and gentle hills—how mild compared to the stern moors of Morton!—greeted my eyes like the features of a once-familiar face. Yes, I recognized this landscape. I was sure we were near Thornfield. "How far is Thornfield Hall from here?" I asked eagerly.
"How far is Thornfield Hall from here?" I asked the stable hand.
"Just two miles, ma'am, across the fields."

"My journey is over," I thought. I got out of the coach and left a trunk in the stable hand's care, to be held until I called for it. I paid my fare, tipped the coachman, and was ready to go. The brightening day shone on the inn's sign, and I read, in gold letters: "The Rochester Arms." My heart leapt—I was already on my master's own land. Then it sank again, as a thought struck me:

"Your master himself may be across the English Channel, for all you know. And if he is at Thornfield Hall, who else is there? His wife—his mad wife. And you have no business with him. You dare not speak to him or seek him out. You've wasted your trip—you'd better go no further," urged my inner voice. "Ask the people at the inn. They can tell you everything you need to know. They can settle your doubts at once. Go up to that man and ask if Mr. Rochester is at home."

The suggestion was sensible, yet I couldn't force myself to act on it. I so dreaded an answer that would crush me with despair. To prolong doubt was to prolong hope. I might yet see the Hall one more time beneath the morning sky. There was the stile before me—the very fields I had stumbled through, blind, deaf, driven half-mad with anguish, on the morning I fled from Thornfield. Before I fully knew what I'd decided, I was in the midst of them. How fast I walked! How eagerly I strained my eyes toward the familiar landscape!

At last the woods rose up. The rookery clustered dark. A loud cawing broke the morning stillness. Strange joy filled me. On I hurried. Another field crossed—a lane threaded—and there were the courtyard walls and the back buildings. The house itself, the rookery still hid. "My first glimpse shall be from the front," I decided, "where the bold battlements will strike my eye at once, and where I can pick out my master's window. Perhaps he'll be standing at it—he rises early. Perhaps he's walking in the orchard, or on the road in front. If so, I could meet him this very minute. Is there not a chance? A possibility?"

I had followed the lower wall of the orchard and turned the corner. There was a gate opening into the meadow, between two stone pillars topped with stone balls. From behind one pillar I could quietly peer around at the full front of the house. I crept forward carefully, wanting to check whether any bedroom blinds had been raised yet. Battlements, windows, the long frontage—all were within my view from this sheltered spot.

The crows sailing overhead may have watched me taking this survey. I wonder what they thought. They must have noticed I was very cautious and timid at first, and that gradually I grew bolder. A peek, then a long stare. Then a departure from my hiding place and a drift into the meadow. Then a sudden stop, full in front of the grand house, and a long, hard look straight at it.
Let me give you an illustration, reader.

A lover finds his beloved asleep on a mossy bank. He wants to catch a glimpse of her face without waking her. He creeps softly over the grass, careful to make no sound. He pauses—thinking she's stirred. He retreats. Not for anything would he be seen. All is still. He advances again. He bends over her. A light veil rests on her features. He lifts it, bends lower. His eyes anticipate the vision of beauty—warm, blooming, lovely in sleep. How quick was his first glance! But how it freezes! How he recoils! Not just a veil was lifted—a mask was removed. What he sees is not his beloved's face—but a skeleton. A death's head, cold and grinning where warmth and beauty should have been.
I looked with fearful hope toward the stately house. I saw a blackened ruin.

No need to hide behind a gatepost now! No need to peer up at windows, fearing someone was stirring behind them! No need to listen for doors opening—to imagine footsteps on the gravel walk! The lawn, the grounds were trampled and overgrown. The front door gaped open and empty. The front of the house was, as I had once seen it in a dream, just a shell—a very high, fragile-looking wall, full of paneless windows. No roof, no battlements, no chimneys—all had collapsed.

And there was the silence of death around it—the solitude of a desolate wasteland. No wonder that letters sent here had never been answered. You might as well have mailed them to a tomb. The black grimness of the stones told how the Hall had fallen—by fire. But how was it started? What story lay behind this disaster? What losses beyond wood and stone and plaster had followed? Had lives been ruined as well as property? If so, whose? Terrible question—one I dreaded having answered, yet felt compelled to ask.

Wandering around the shattered walls and through the devastated interior, I gathered evidence that the catastrophe was not recent. Winter snows had drifted through that empty arch. Winter rains had beaten in through hollow windows. Among the soaked piles of rubble, spring had encouraged new growth—grass and weeds sprouted between the stones and fallen beams. And where, in the meantime, was the unfortunate owner of this wreck? In what country? Under what circumstances? My eyes wandered over the grey, neglected ruins. Then they instinctively turned toward the sky above the ruins, as if searching for something more.

I needed answers. I could find them only at the inn. I returned there before long. The innkeeper brought my breakfast to the parlour. I asked him to close the door and sit down. I had questions. But when he did as I asked, I hardly knew how to begin. I dreaded the possible answers so much. Yet the scene of destruction I had just witnessed had partially prepared me for bad news. The innkeeper was a respectable-looking, middle-aged man.
"You know Thornfield Hall, of course?" I finally managed to say.
"Yes, ma'am. I lived there once."
"Did you?" Not during my time, I thought. You're a stranger to me.
"I was the late Mr. Rochester's butler," he added.
The late! The words hit me with the full force of the blow I'd been trying to dodge.
"The late!" I gasped. "Is he dead?"

"I mean the present gentleman, Mr. Edward's father," he explained. I breathed again. My blood flowed once more. Those words fully assured me that Mr. Edward—my Mr. Rochester, God bless him wherever he was!—was at least alive. Was, in fact, "the present gentleman." What comforting words! It seemed I could now bear whatever came next—whatever the revelations might be—with relative calm. Since he was not in the grave, I could endure hearing he was at the other end of the earth.
"Is Mr. Rochester living at Thornfield Hall now?" I asked, knowing what the answer would be, but wanting to delay the direct question about where he actually was.

"No, ma'am—oh no! No one's living there. I suppose you're a stranger to these parts, or you'd have heard what happened last autumn. Thornfield Hall is a complete ruin. It burned down around harvest time. A terrible disaster! So much valuable property destroyed—hardly any furniture saved. The fire broke out in the middle of the night. By the time the fire engines arrived from Millcote, the building was a mass of flames. It was a terrible sight. I saw it myself."
"In the middle of the night!" I murmured. Yes, that was always the fateful hour at Thornfield. "Was it known how the fire started?" I asked.

"They guessed, ma'am—they guessed. In fact, I'd say it was proven beyond doubt. You may not be aware," he continued, pulling his chair closer to the table and speaking low, "that there was a lady—a lunatic—kept in the house?"
"I've heard something about it."

"She was kept in very strict confinement, ma'am. For years, people weren't even certain she existed. No one saw her. They only knew by rumor that such a person was at the Hall. Who or what she was, nobody could figure out. They said Mr. Edward had brought her from abroad. Some believed she had been his mistress. But then a strange thing happened about a year ago—a very strange thing."
I was afraid of hearing my own story. I tried to steer him back to the main point.
"And this lady?"
"This lady, ma'am," he answered, "turned out to be Mr. Rochester's wife! The discovery happened in the strangest way. There was a young lady, a governess at the Hall, that Mr. Rochester fell in—"
"But the fire," I prompted.

"I'm coming to that, ma'am. Mr. Edward fell in love with her. The servants said they'd never seen anyone so smitten. He followed her everywhere. They used to watch him—servants do, you know, ma'am—and he was devoted to her beyond everything. Though nobody but him thought her all that beautiful. She was a little, small thing, they said—almost like a child. I never saw her myself, but I heard Leah the housemaid talk about her. Leah liked her well enough. Mr. Rochester was about forty, and she was barely twenty. You see, when gentlemen his age fall in love with girls, they're often like men bewitched. Well, he would marry her."
"You'll tell me that part another time," I said. "Right now I particularly want to hear about the fire. Was it suspected that Mrs. Rochester had anything to do with it?"

"You've hit it, ma'am. It's quite certain it was her—and nobody else—who started it. She had a woman looking after her called Mrs. Poole—an able woman in her line, very trustworthy, except for one weakness. A weakness common to many nurses—she kept a private bottle of gin by her, and now and then had a drop too much. That's understandable, given the hard life she led. But it was dangerous, because when Mrs. Poole was fast asleep after the gin, the madwoman—cunning as a witch—would take the keys from her pocket, let herself out of her room, and wander the house doing whatever wild mischief came into her head. They say she once nearly burned her husband in his bed—but I don't know about that. Anyway, on this night, she set fire first to the hangings in the room next to her own, then made her way down to a lower floor, to the chamber that had been the governess's—as if she somehow knew how matters stood, and had a grudge against her—and set fire to the bed there. But luckily nobody was sleeping in it. The governess had run off two months before, and though Mr. Rochester searched for her as if she were the most precious thing he had in the world, he could never learn a word of her whereabouts. He grew savage—truly savage—over the disappointment. He'd never been a wild man, but he turned dangerous after he lost her. He wanted to be alone, too. He sent Mrs. Fairfax, the housekeeper, away to live with friends at a distance—but he did it handsomely, settling an annuity on her for life, and she deserved it, being a very good woman. Miss Adèle, a ward of his, was sent off to school. He broke off with all the local gentry and shut himself up at the Hall like a hermit."
"What! He didn't leave England?"

"Leave England? God, no! He wouldn't so much as cross the doorstep—except at night, when he'd walk like a ghost around the grounds and through the orchard. As if he'd lost his mind—which, in my opinion, he had. Because before that slip of a governess crossed his path, you'd never have met a more spirited, bolder, keener gentleman. He wasn't a man given to drinking, gambling, or horse racing, as some are, and he wasn't especially handsome. But he had courage and a will of his own, if ever a man did. I knew him from a boy, you see—and for my part, I've often wished Miss Eyre had been sunk in the sea before she ever came to Thornfield Hall."
"Then Mr. Rochester was at home when the fire broke out?"

"Yes, indeed. And he went up to the attics when everything was burning above and below. He got the servants out of their beds and helped them down himself. Then he went back to get his wife out of her room. And then they called up to him that she was on the roof. She was standing there, waving her arms above the battlements, shouting so loud they could hear her a mile away. I saw her and heard her with my own eyes and ears. She was a big woman, with long black hair. We could see it streaming against the flames as she stood there. I heard Mr. Rochester call to her. I saw him climb through the skylight onto the roof. We shouted for him to come down—it was too dangerous. He approached her. Then she yelled, and with one leap she was over the edge—"
The next moment she lay smashed on the pavement.
"Dead?"
"Dead! As dead as the stones her brains and blood were scattered on."
"Good God!"
"You may well say so, ma'am. It was horrifying!"
He shuddered.
"And afterward?" I pressed.
"Well, ma'am, afterward the house burned to the ground. Only some bits of walls are standing now."
"Were any other lives lost?"
"No—perhaps it would have been better if there had."
"What do you mean?"

"Poor Mr. Edward!" he burst out. "I never thought I'd see the day! Some say it was God's judgment on him for keeping his first marriage secret and trying to take another wife while she was alive. But I pity him, for my part."
"You said he's alive?" I exclaimed.
"Yes, yes, he's alive. But many think he'd be better off dead."
"Why? How?" My blood ran cold again. "Where is he? Is he in England?"
"Yes—he's in England. He can't get out of England, I imagine—he's stuck now."
What agony! And the man seemed determined to draw it out.
"He is stone-blind," he said at last. "Yes—stone-blind is Mr. Edward."
I had feared worse. I had feared he was mad. I summoned strength to ask what had caused this.

"It was his own courage, and you might say his kindness, in a way, ma'am. He wouldn't leave the house till everyone else was out. As he came down the great staircase after Mrs. Rochester threw herself from the battlements, there was a massive crash—everything collapsed. He was pulled from the ruins alive, but badly injured. A beam had partly protected him, but one eye was destroyed, and one hand was so crushed that the surgeon, Mr. Carter, had to amputate it immediately. He lost the other eye too. He's now helpless—blind and crippled."
"Where is he? Where does he live now?"
"At Ferndean, a manor house on a farm he owns, about thirty miles away. Quite a desolate place."
"Who is with him?"
"Old John and his wife. He wouldn't have anyone else. He's quite broken down, they say."
"Have you any kind of vehicle?"
"We have a chaise, ma'am—a very fine chaise."
"Have it ready at once. If your driver can get me to Ferndean before dark today, I'll pay you both double the usual rate."
